extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of logic, philosophy, and scientific methodology
extracted.subtask_description: Theory and systematic criteria for (a) arranging natural groups into a series to aid particular inductive inquiries, and (b) classifying the varieties of fallacious apparent evidence (fallacies) that mislead reasoning. Includes diagnostic guidance for detecting errors in inference and observation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification for a particular inductive inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: The requisites of a classification intended to facilitate the study of a particular phenomenon: first, bring into one class all kinds of things which exhibit that phenomenon (in whatever variety of forms or degrees); secondly, arrange those kinds in a series according to the degree in which they exhibit it, beginning with those which exhibit most and terminating with those which exhibit least.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This arrangement places instances in the order implied by the Method of Concomitant Variations (fourth Method). It is intended to make simultaneous contemplation of cases most likely to throw light on laws of the phenomenon. Use when the purpose is to facilitate a particular inductive inquiry rather than general grouping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply the Method of Concomitant Variations (order by degree)
rubrics_metrics.description: To infer laws when artificial experiments are limited, put instances in an order according to degrees in which they exhibit the phenomenon; facts that increase or diminish together suggest causal relations (cause-effect or common cause).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The formation of such a series should precede applying the Method of Concomitant Variations. The principle: 'facts which increase or diminish together, and disappear together, are either cause and effect, or effects of a common cause.' Use series to support inductions where controlled experiments are impracticable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assume a type-species (type as exemplar)
rubrics_metrics.description: To recognize the identity of a phenomenon across degrees, assume a type-species: consider as the type the kind which exhibits the constitutive properties of the class in the highest degree; conceive other varieties as deviations by inferior intensity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The highest-intensity instance is where subordinate phenomena and joint-effects are most apparent, aiding recognition of their rudiments in lesser instances. The assumption of a type-species is 'indispensable' for apprehending a natural series.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary divisions grounded on variations in degree of the main phenomenon
rubrics_metrics.description: The primary divisions of a series must be founded not on all distinctions indiscriminately but on those that correspond to variations in the degree of the main phenomenon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Groups must be natural affinities and should not place together things that occupy different points of the general scale. Break the series where variation in intensity of the main phenomenon begins to be attended by conspicuous changes in miscellaneous properties (e.g., where Mammalia ends).

rubrics_metrics.name: Subdivisions (families/genera) should be contiguous in the general scale
rubrics_metrics.description: Families and genera, where possible, should be subdivided so that portions stand higher and lower (though contiguous) in the general scale; only when impossible is it allowable to ground subdivisions on characters having no determinable connection with the main phenomenon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This preserves the integrity of the natural series and avoids mixing ranks from different positions on the scale. When impossible, note the limitation and justify alternative characters used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form groups according to the most important characters (principal phenomenon predominates)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a principal phenomenon transcends other properties in importance, form groups principally by the characters that reflect that phenomenon; other properties may be regarded as modifications of it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This guards against undue emphasis on incidental properties (example: Cuvier's overemphasis on alimentation). The chief criterion is how much a character contributes to the main phenomenon's laws and history.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply natural-arrangement principles beyond natural history
rubrics_metrics.description: The principles of natural arrangement (grouping and series construction) apply to other domains—art, business, codification of laws—where parts of an extensive subject must be brought into mental co-ordination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study and practice on biological classification (animals) is a recommended preparatory discipline for other classification tasks (Bentham's codification example). The same scientific conditions govern proper arrangement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Catalogue fallacies as varieties of apparent but not real evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: A fallacy is a variety of apparent evidence which is not real evidence; the aim is to enumerate the varieties of apparent evidence that are liable to be mistaken for real evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify fallacies either by the cause that makes them appear evidentiary or by the particular kind of evidence which they simulate. The focus is on the manner in which people come to entertain false conclusions, not on the false opinions themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish Fallacies of Simple Inspection (a priori) from Fallacies of Inference
rubrics_metrics.description: Fallacies of Simple Inspection (a priori) are cases where a proposition is believed or a presumption is created by inspection alone—either literally held without extrinsic evidence or given a presumption sufficient to dispense with strict induction. Fallacies of Inference are erroneous conclusions drawn from supposed evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place Natural Prejudices and 'a priori' fallacies at the head of classifications. When a presumption exists that is strong enough to prevent rigorous induction, treat it as a Fallacy of Simple Inspection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fallacies of Confusion (errors from shifting or vague premises)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fallacies of Confusion arise when premises are not conceived with due fixity: one conception of the evidence is formed when collected and another when used; includes errors from vagueness, ambiguity of terms, or casual associations in language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These often surface as equivocation, suppressed shifts in meaning, or substitution of different premises/conclusions during reasoning. Identify ambiguous terms and fix precise meanings to diagnose such fallacies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-division: Apparent evidence may simulate Induction or Deduction
rubrics_metrics.description: Apparent evidence can simulate either simple Induction (particular facts) or Deduction (foregone generalizations); further, the evidence (facts or general propositions) may be false or true but inconclusive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This yields classes: Fallacies of Induction and Fallacies of Deduction, each subdivided according to whether the supposed evidence is false or true-but-insufficient. Analyze both the form of argument and the truth/sufficiency of premises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fallacies of Observation (inductive errors from erroneous facts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fallacies of Observation are inductive fallacies where the facts on which induction proceeds are erroneous—malobservation, non-observation, or indirect reliance on intermediate marks that do not prove what they are supposed to prove.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Errors may stem from direct misobservation or from inferring false facts by mistaken proxies. Remedy by more careful observation, verification, and checking intermediate inferential steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fallacies of Generalization (inductive errors from insufficient facts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fallacies of Generalization occur when the facts are correct but the conclusion is not warranted by them—overgeneralizing from inadequate samples or incomplete induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify subordinate groups of such fallacies (to be enumerated elsewhere); guard against hasty generalization and ensure adequate, representative sampling and proper scope conditions before generalizing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fallacies of Deduction and Fallacies of Ratiocination
rubrics_metrics.description: Among deductive fallacies, those with false general premises fall under inductive/error-in-premises heads; the remaining deductive fallacies are those in which the premises (even if true) do not support the conclusion—termed Fallacies of Ratiocination (vicious argumentation violating rules of the syllogism).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detect by testing whether premises logically entail the conclusion; when argument is set out explicitly, such fallacies reduce to recognized violations of valid syllogistic forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify fallacies by whether the supposed connection is inferential or admitted on inspection
rubrics_metrics.description: The supposed connection between two facts may be concluded from other evidence or admitted without ground; this distinction underlies the primary split between inferential fallacies and a priori (inspection) fallacies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When diagnosing an error, ask whether the arguer claims empirical or logical grounds for the connection, or merely a self-evident presumption; the remedial approach differs accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Error originates from assuming habitual conjunctions (groundless general propositions)
rubrics_metrics.description: When we regard one fact as evidentiary of another incorrectly, it is because we have admitted, explicitly or tacitly, a groundless general proposition about their conjunction—believing that A is habitually conjoined with B when it is not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expose and test any implicit generalization about co-occurrence; require evidence for claimed regular conjunctions before inferring dependence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish accidental lapses from fundamental methodological errors
rubrics_metrics.description: Exclude mere casual lapses (errors from hurry or inattention) from the category of fallacies that require philosophical analysis; focus on modes of performing reasoning fundamentally wrong rather than inexpertness in application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Casual mistakes are remedied by attention and practice; the work of classifying fallacies aims at systematic, recurrent errors that persist despite attention and require conceptual remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical detection: supply suppressed premises and clarify tacit steps
rubrics_metrics.description: In many real arguments links are suppressed or tacit; to detect fallacies supply the suppressed premises—the error often lurks in tacit or half-conscious steps. Socratic interrogation can force the arguer to state assumptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask the arguer to state all premises explicitly. If a suppressed premise is dubious or false, the supposed inference collapses. This method commonly exposes sophistry or unexamined assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope exclusion: moral causes of erroneous belief are indirect and excluded from logical taxonomy
rubrics_metrics.description: Moral causes (indifference to truth, bias, wishes) are not direct sources of wrong conclusions in this taxonomy; they operate indirectly by perverting intellectual grounds and thus will be encompassed only insofar as they produce intellectual fallacies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing fallacies, attribute errors to the intellectual mechanism that admitted insufficient evidence; treat moral influences as background predisposing causes rather than primary logical species.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safeguard: cultivate habit of reasoning well (familiarity + practice)
rubrics_metrics.description: The only complete safeguard against reasoning ill is the habit of reasoning well—familiarity with the principles of correct reasoning and practice in applying them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Training and practice in rigorous induction and explicit testing of evidence reduce susceptibility to fallacies. Education should include exposure to the catalog of fallacies to 'make the mind feel its weaknesses'.
